title: { 🌱: "One year !"}
author: Franck Pachot
body_html:
A year ago, I joined MongoDB, a NoSQL database company, after spending my career exclusively with SQL databases. Many saw it as a significant change, almost like switching football teams. But it wasn’t. While it’s a different type of database, it still aligns with the same core goals I’ve focused on for 30 years: processing, storing, and sharing application data, all while ensuring good and predictable performance, high availability, and a smooth developer experience for the best productivity in development and deployment.

For me, it felt more like continuing an ongoing journey in databases:

  • Gaining a deeper understanding of developers. I was already moving away from the typical SQL DBA mindset that criticizes ORMs without considering the development challenges they address. Helping users with document modeling was the next step: once you understand domain-driven design, having a dedicated database per domain makes sense, and using the domain model directly, rather than normalizing and mapping it with an ORM, is often a good start.
  • Exploring horizontal scalability further. I began understanding clustering and replication in Oracle and PostgreSQL, then advanced to consensus protocols and multi-region deployments with YugabyteDB. At MongoDB, I deepened this knowledge, as sharding and consensus-based replication are at the core of the product and tunable for various topologies. The research and engineering teams at MongoDB include top experts, perhaps too modest in public sharing.
  • Learning more about storage engine trade-offs, such as B-trees vs. LSM trees, optimistic vs. pessimistic locking, MVCC implementations, and logical vs. physical replication. I was most surprised to discover how advanced WiredTiger, MongoDB’s storage engine, truly is—among the most sophisticated I’ve encountered in B-tree flexibility, failure resilience, lock-free concurrency control, and hybrid workloads performance.

I aim to share my learnings through blog posts, videos, presentations, and social media. Instead of looking for a single "best" database, I prefer to compare different approaches, their trade-offs, and distinguish between what is based on facts and what is based on myths. There’s no universal database. What’s important is understanding how each works, and the best database for you is the one you understand and use effectively. Devrel’s role isn’t to force a choice, but to bring awareness and help you succeed with your choice. I also challenge myths and biased benchmarks, especially those that persist among SQL-only experts, often based on outdated information or misconceptions from the early days of NoSQL. All databases have evolved significantly over the past few years.

This one-year experience is about more than technology. It’s also about the company and my role. I’ve never seen such rapid change, which reflects how MongoDB’s flexible schema mindset extends throughout the organization. In just a year, some original team members who brought me in have moved to other database companies, new colleagues have arrived, and we’ve had changes in CFO, CMO, and even CEO. Yet the team’s spirit has remained strong and consistent, the product has evolved quickly, and the stock market has validated these evolutions.

While I’ve been a developer advocate before, this is my first role within a marketing department. I thought it would have been the most challenging transition—more so than changing companies or technologies—because I see DevRel as helping users and the community make informed decisions, promoting technology only when it truly benefits them. Previously, I reported to the CTO and was part of product management, not marketing. I wasn't sure about having the same freedom in a marketing department. However, MongoDB encourages honest, fact-based messaging. In my year here, I have not once been told what I should or should not say in my publications. I also engage freely with product teams, solution architects, champions, and customers, offering help where my knowledge of MongoDB and SQL makes sense—never as a sales tactic.

What I value most about MongoDB as a company is its openness. When I started discussions a year ago, I had no intention of leaving Yugabyte, which is a great company with strong technology. But I was excited by the challenge of a different database and by MongoDB’s willingness to hire people with diverse viewpoints and messages, rather than remain in the NoSQL echo chamber. Building on my extensive SQL experience, my goal is to help developers choose the document model thoughtfully, use it appropriately, and be clear about when it’s not the best fit—when normalization and relational databases may be the better option. There is still a lot to do in the database world, and no single database is best for every situation.

Getting feedback is a major part of devrel, so please continue engagements and discussions on all platforms.
